subject: Business
title: Customer Discovery Interviews
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Customer Discovery Interviews.

hook.text: You think you know what customers want. Talk to five of them and everything changes.

buildup.text: Customer discovery means asking open-ended questions about problems — not pitching your solution.

discovery.text: The Mom Test: never ask 'Would you use this?' People lie to be nice. Ask about past behavior.

twist.text: The best insights come from complaints. 'What's the hardest part about X?' reveals real pain.

climax.text: Five good interviews often reveal more than a 500-person survey. Depth beats breadth early on.

quiz.question: What does The Mom Test advise against asking?
options: 'What's the hardest part of your workflow?'
'When did you last face this problem?'

details.summary: Customer discovery interviews systematically validate assumptions about customer problems, behaviors, and willingness to pay before building solutions. Steve Blank's methodology requires talking to potential customers not to pitch but to learn whether the problem you plan to solve actually exists.
details.whyItMatters: Most startups fail by building solutions for problems that do not exist or that customers will not pay to solve. Customer discovery interviews are the cheapest and fastest way to validate whether your assumptions about the market match reality.
takeaways: Interview customers to learn about their problems, not to pitch your solution
Ask about past behavior rather than hypothetical interest for reliable insights
Customer discovery should happen before any significant product development

faq.question: What questions should you ask in customer discovery interviews?
faq.answer: Ask about their current process and pain points. What have they tried? How much time and money do they spend on the problem now? Avoid asking would you buy this, because people say yes to be polite. Instead ask about past behavior and current spending, which reveals real willingness to pay.

faq.question: How many customer interviews do you need before drawing conclusions?
faq.answer: Typically 20 to 30 interviews reveal clear patterns. If you hear the same problems repeatedly after 10 conversations, you are likely on track. If every conversation reveals different problems, your target customer is too broad. Continue until new interviews stop revealing surprising information.
